item.title: Digging up the past can change the ground beneath it
item.description: Archaeological excavation uncovers the past but also changes the landscape that has preserved sites for centuries or millennia. These changes influence water flow, soil erosion and the stability of exposed remains. Researchers from Istanbul Technical University and the U.S. have shown how computer models can assist archaeologists in understanding and planning for these effects, especially regarding erosion risks. Using an Early Bronze Age settlement in Türkiye as a case study, they reconstructed the landscape before and after excavation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: UN climate summit prepares to host world leaders from more than 90 countries tomorrow As Turkey convenes world leaders to forge agreements that stop climate breakdown, its own leader is celebrating new fossil fuel exploration. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, who is expected at Cop31 in Antalya later today, announced the “encouraging” discovery of two new oilfields in the Gabar mountains in a post on X last night. item.title: Heat-trapping carbon pollution drops, but scientists cite the Iran war rather than energy progress
item.description: In 2026, the world emitted 42.2 billion tonne of heat-trapping carbon dioxide from the burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas. It's a 0.4% decrease from last year, according to the scientists of the Global Carbon Project Publicado también por: The Hindu - International. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fossil fuel emissions set to fall for first time since Covid, research shows
item.description: Global fossil fuel emissions are expected to fall by 0.4 percent in 2026 for first time since the Covid pandemic, driven by the expansion of renewable energy and the oil price shock linked to the Iran war, researchers said Tuesday, who warned the decline may be short-lived. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE 24

item.description: A medida que crece la capacidad para viajar más lejos en el espacio, lo hace también la necesidad de buscar nuevos propelentes. Por ejemplo, cada vez hay más empresas y agencias investigando la propulsión nuclear . No obstante, también se puede recurrir al reabastecimiento, ya sea mediante naves que actúan como gasolineras espaciales o a través del uso de combustibles que puedan obtenerse directamente en la Luna y otros lugares del Sistema Solar. En esa línea, el agua sería un propelente logísticamente muy interesante. Usarla para impulsar naves por el espacio puede parecer una locura, pero a… Fuente: Xataka.

item.description: Low clouds trace the branching valleys of the Appalachian Plateau and the Cumberland River, then burn off by afternoon. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Math anxiety may be stopping students from learning useful AI and data skills
item.description: Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming part of everyday life and work. AI can generate information, summarize evidence and perform calculations. However, it does not remove the need for critical thinking and conceptual understanding. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Light-pulse pairs reveal the femtosecond decay of an inner-shell hole in xenon atoms
item.description: Researchers at the UVSOR Synchrotron Facility (Institute for Molecular Science, Japan) and partner institutions have observed the decay of a xenon 4d core hole, an inner-shell vacancy, directly in the time domain. They used pairs of phase-coherent extreme ultraviolet pulses from a synchrotron to make the photoelectron wave packets they released interfere. The contrast of the interference fringes decreased over a few femtoseconds as the delay between the pulses increased. A model using literature core-hole lifetimes of about 6 femtoseconds reproduced this rapid decay of the fringe contrast… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI-assisted atomic models reveal how protective shells regulate aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
item.description: Building an accurate model of how atoms interact is a complicated process. Researchers must choose new calculations, test successive models and track the mechanisms behind each interaction. But a newly developed AI agent called MLP Copilot has made this process much easier by bridging computational tools and scientific evidence with human supervision. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
item.description: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Barium titanate's optical properties emerge more clearly after decades of widely varying measurements
item.description: A KAIST-led research team has characterized how light propagates through and is absorbed by barium titanate (BTO), a promising material for next-generation optical communication devices. By clarifying optical properties that had been difficult to determine because of the material's complex internal structure, the study provides a foundation for designing these devices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Electrical technique concentrates milk without using heat, challenging traditional preservation methods
item.description: Dehydrating milk to turn it into powder is, today, an energy-intensive process that subjects the product to high temperatures. Powdered milk is widely used by the food industry and allows the product to be stored and transported in a stable condition for long periods of time without the need for refrigeration. While industrial methods are effective, they have high energy costs and can alter heat-sensitive components, such as whey proteins, enzymes or vitamins. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fossil CO₂ emissions projected to decrease in 2026 amid clean energy growth and Iran conflict
item.description: Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0.4% in 2026—driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict—according to new research by the Global Carbon Project. The 2026 edition (the 21st annual report) is published in the journal Earth System Science Data. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The surprising power of connecting with strangers
item.description: You're walking through the farmers market with a screaming toddler tucked under your arm football style. You're tired, you're leaving without the produce you came for and you're embarrassed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: After 40 years, CERN finds evidence of a one-in-10-billion particle decay
item.description: CERN scientists have finally found evidence of a particle decay so rare that it happens only once in roughly 10 billion decays, ending a search spanning more than 40 years. The breakthrough could help physicists uncover hidden particles and forces that lie beyond the reach of today's most powerful accelerators. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Gatineau Park foliage reveals local Cold War nuclear testing legacy
item.description: For more than six decades, local scientists have collected sugar maple leaves from Gatineau Park to measure their radiocarbon levels, creating the longest continuous record of its kind. Now, a study of those leaves led by the André E. Lalonde National Facility for Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AEL-AMS) located at the University of Ottawa shows that the effects of Cold War–era nuclear weapons testing have only recently disappeared from the local biosphere. The study, titled "Stored carbohydrates buffer Bomb and Suess radiocarbon effects in maple leaves across a 65-year Ottawa region record,"… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Accidental discovery enables room-temperature recrystallization of molybdenum
item.description: Researchers at the University of Rochester and Technion–Israel Institute of Technology accidentally discovered a new way to rearrange the internal structure of molybdenum—an extremely heat-resistant metal—at room temperature. Molybdenum is typically used to reinforce nuclear reactors, jet engine turbine blades and rocket nozzles because it doesn't melt until it is heated to more than 2,600°C (4,712°F). Controlling its atomic structure at room temperature could open the door to more applications, including next-generation semiconductors. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study identifies single amino acid change that alters Andes virus protein behavior in human cells
item.description: Mount Sinai researchers have identified a single amino acid difference between rodent- and human-derived Andes virus isolates that changes how a key viral protein behaves inside human cells. The findings help explain biological differences between closely related virus isolates. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Starling numbers are declining—we're investigating whether their spectacular murmuration displays are changing too
item.description: Every autumn, from city centers to wetlands, starling murmurations attract crowds of spectators. Thousands of birds fill the sky, twisting and turning in extraordinary waves as the sun sets. An entire flock moves as one, creating shapes that shift and dissolve as quickly as they appear. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Methane-eating microbes grown on electrodes build electrically conductive nanowires
item.description: Certain microorganisms (anaerobic methanotrophic archaea, or ANME) consume methane and convert it into electricity, as research conducted four years ago by microbiologist Cornelia Welte of Radboud University revealed. New research by Welte and her colleagues published in Nature Communications now shows that these methane-consuming organisms do this by producing nanowires through which they can transmit the electricity they generate. The researchers have also succeeded in cultivating these specific microorganisms in almost pure form in the lab. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cracking the case of the Roman frog graveyard
item.description: Ten years after 8,000 ancient frog bones were discovered in a single ditch, scientists at Bournemouth University and the Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) have finally identified the culprits Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Anglo-Saxon kingdom chose copper coins despite abundant silver
item.description: Analysis of silver and gold from the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Northumbria finds that, contrary to popular belief, it did not suffer from a shortage of precious metals, questioning why the kingdom used copper-alloy coins rather than silver like its contemporaries. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Water may play critical role in how our tissues stretch and spring back
item.description: Every time your heart beats, your lungs expand, or your skin stretches, a remarkable protein called elastin helps your body return to its original shape. But what exactly gives this protein its elasticity? For more than 50 years, scientists have debated whether elastin's ability to stretch and recoil comes primarily from the protein's own flexibility or from its interactions with surrounding water molecules. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Archaeological finds at an Irish fort reveal insights into the finer side of medieval life
item.description: Popular media, from computer games to movies, often portray medieval life as being dominated by fighters and farmers. In these depictions, there's little evidence of a world beyond political struggle and simple subsistence. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Endangered leatherbacks find new nesting beaches in Ecuador as Pacific Ocean warms
item.description: A hopeful story for the world's largest, critically endangered sea turtle may be playing out along the sandy beaches of Ecuador. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Machine learning reveals how often fish schooling evolved—and repeatedly disappeared
item.description: Scientists have used new machine learning techniques to investigate a topic no one has ever found a way to study: the evolution of fish moving together in schools across thousands of species. The new paper, published Nov. 6 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, is among the largest studies of the evolution of any behavior ever conducted in any group of species, according to the authors. The research shows that behaviors, which have previously been difficult to quantify, can be studied at a large evolutionary scale. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tin deposits are formed from source rocks, not cooling
item.description: New research from the University of St Andrews has uncovered the primary drivers of tin mineralization, which will have significant implications for the discovery of tin deposits critical to the energy transition. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A parasite linked to cats may also threaten dogs' eyesight, researchers find
item.description: A parasitic infection commonly associated with cats may be associated with severe, potentially sight-threatening ocular disease in dogs, according to a new study by researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a hidden gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that helps explain why bitter coffee and other initially unpleasant flavors can become favorites over time. The discovery reveals how the brain learns to crave certain foods and could eventually lead to new ways of reshaping eating habits and food preferences. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Tree-rich landscapes help birds and bats nearly double cacao yields in Peru
item.description: Tropical farmers are often expected to choose between high crop yields and protecting wildlife. However, an international team of researchers led by the University of Vienna, in collaboration with the universities of Göttingen and Würzburg in Germany and Bioversity International in Peru, shows that biodiversity conservation reinforces cacao production in agroforests via associated ecosystem services, such as natural pest control. The new study, published in Communications Earth & Environment, provides important evidence for sustainable farm and landscape management in one of the world's most… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The ELT can probe ultra-diffuse galaxies and their dark matter mysteries
item.description: We've been waiting a long time for the Extremely Large Telescope's first light, scheduled for March 2029. Telescopes this large, powerful and costly always have multiple science goals, and that's true for the ELT. One of its science goals is to study fundamental aspects of the universe, including dark matter. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Did early humans collect keepsakes 500,000 years ago?
item.description: Most of us are familiar with the urge to pick up a seashell from the beach or keep a stone from a hiking trip. The object itself may be ordinary, but to the person who keeps it, it serves as a reminder of a particular moment, place or person. Where did this behavior come from? Did early humans do the same? A new study by Tel Aviv University researchers suggests that this practice stretches back approximately half a million years, with important consequences for the evolution of memory. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Some regions may already be living in a 1.5°C warmer world
item.description: Regions worldwide may have already experienced around 90%–94% of the warming expected when the global average reaches 1.5°C above preindustrial levels, and 65%–76% of that expected at 2°C of warming. The findings, published in Nature Climate Change, suggest that regional warming in 2025 was statistically indistinguishable from the levels expected in a 1.5°C warmer world, underlining the immediate need for adaptation across all regions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rocket Lab shares dip after the company’s ‘defining’ quarter misses the mark
item.description: The rocket-launch company just posted a steeper loss than analysts were expecting. Fuente: MarketWatch.

item.title: Male lizard 'perfumes' may be more about rivalry than seduction
item.description: Animals communicate in ways that are sometimes obvious to us and sometimes almost completely hidden. Bright colors, songs and courtship displays are easy to notice. Chemical signals are different: an animal can leave a message behind long after it has moved away. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A stellar odd couple at an unusual stage of evolution
item.description: Most of the stars in the Milky Way are what we might call normal stars. They're main sequence stars like our sun, meaning they're doing what most people probably think stars do: shining as they fuse hydrogen atoms into helium atoms on a vast scale. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Upgraded microscope can now watch individual quantum particles in motion
item.description: Energy can be carried in a number of ways: by electrons, the particles that underpin all modern electronics, as well as by quasiparticles, the results of different particles interacting with one another at the quantum level. Columbia chemist Milan Delor has been watching these different forms of energy flow with an instrument called stroboSCAT, a unique microscope that uses strobe-like light pulses to capture particles and quasiparticles as they move through different materials. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Newest Sample, Oldest Rock?
item.description: Written by Tasha Coelho, Mastcam-Z Student Collaborator at Arizona State University Nov. 1, 2026 Perseverance’s most recent abrasion “Pumbe” bears a striking resemblance to an earlier abrasion, “Badger Peak.” That’s no coincidence. As previously reported, that rock had a hardness too high to core. However, the team felt strongly that it was worth the effort […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: New perovskite system extends room-temperature spin polarization via successive quantum wells
item.description: A research team led by Lu Haipeng, a professor in the Department of Chemistry at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), has achieved a breakthrough in preserving spin information for optoelectronic technologies. The team has developed a perovskite chiral multiple quantum-well system that maintains spin polarization approximately 300 times longer at room temperature. The study opens new possibilities for future quantum technologies and next-generation spin-based applications. The study was published in the journal Nature Photonics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Computer science researcher reroutes truckloads of excess food from landfills to food pantries
item.description: The planet already grows enough food to feed everyone. The problem is one of logistics. A third of all the food grown and raised goes to waste, meaning that one in 12 people does not have enough to eat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Subaru Telescope reveals the shape and temperature of Comet Encke's nucleus
item.description: Mid-infrared observations with the Subaru Telescope have revealed the shape and surface temperature of the nucleus of Comet 2P/Encke. By analyzing how the nucleus's thermal emission changed as it rotated, the researchers found that the nucleus is elongated, with a long axis of about 7 kilometers and a short axis of about 3 kilometers. They also determined that the surface temperature at the time of observation was 328 ± 7 Kelvin (about 55°C). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Light reflecting within thin films can masquerade as molecular signals in perovskite solar materials
item.description: An infrared signal thought to reveal how molecules in perovskite solar materials respond to light-generated charges can arise largely from the way light travels through the thin film itself, a new theoretical study shows. Jun Nishida, assistant professor at the Institute for Molecular Science (IMS), Japan, found that light-generated charges alter how infrared light is reflected and transmitted within the film layers, producing sharp features that resemble changes in molecular vibrations even when the vibrations themselves are unaltered. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: COP31 opens amid energy crisis as activists demand climate action
item.description: COP31 has opened in Turkiye amid war-driven energy disruptions and a renewed reliance on fossil fuels. Fuente: Al Jazeera English.

item.title: NASA’s Chandra Finds Source of Star’s Mysterious Outbursts
item.description: Using NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, astronomers have discovered what is triggering repeated outbursts from a giant, unstable star. A new study, published Monday in the latest issue of The Astrophysical Journal, details the discovery of a previously hidden companion object that keeps pulling material away from the massive star every 113 days as they orbit […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: High-pressure setup unlocks detailed measurements of organized structures in turbulent flows
item.description: Turbulent flows are ubiquitous: they are found in clouds, in the ocean and even on other planets. Yet despite their chaotic nature, they also form large-scale structures that can be calculated and predicted. For example, while long streaks of clouds may appear orderly from the outside, their interiors are characterized by intense turbulence. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Knowing how plants stretch out when warm could help dial back their response
item.description: When they start to get too warm but before they're dangerously hot, most plants employ a similar playbook. They change their shape, a host of adaptations that includes growing longer stems and stalks to promote air circulation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study reveals overcompensation in desert plant-weevil interactions
item.description: A research team led by professor Zhang Yuanming from the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography (XIEG) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has revealed that the outcomes of desert plant-herbivore interactions are strongly context-dependent. The paper is published in the journal Plant, Cell & Environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Genetic hitchhikers make Aspergillus infections even harder to treat
item.description: Resistance to antifungal medicines in the pathogenic fungus Aspergillus fumigatus is proving more persistent than previously thought. Research by Wageningen University & Research (WUR), published in Current Biology, shows that fungicides used in agriculture, even those with a different mode of action from these medicines, can help maintain this resistance. This is because different resistance genes "hitchhike" together. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 2026 set to be one of the 4 hottest years on record
item.description: The year 2026 continues the protracted streak of exceptional global temperatures, melting ice and rising sea levels, with a very strong El Niño event set to unleash even more heat and extreme weather well into 2027, according to a new report from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). It highlights the knock-on risks to the environment, economy and everyday life. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Quantum interference keeps two atoms bound despite enough energy to break apart
item.description: How can something remain intact when it should naturally break apart? This question has been addressed by researchers at RPTU. Their work has led to the experimental observation of an unusual quantum state in which two atoms remain bound together even though they possess enough energy to separate. The results have been published in the journal Nature Physics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Show HN: Every satellite that passed over any place this week, and its photos
item.description: hey HN, i built this because i wanted to know what had actually photographed my street. type in any place and it finds every satellite that passed over it in the last 7 days (SGP4 on the CelesTrak catalog, runs in your browser in about half a second), then pulls the real Sentinel-2 / Landsat / NASA images from those passes. some fun bits: - the pass search can't skip a pass. checked it against a brute force on poles, the antimeridian and tiny swaths: 0 missed - all ~17k objects in orbit are drawn on the GPU, solving Kepler's equation every frame - Sentinel-2 timestamps are often 5-10 min off… Fuente: Hacker News - Portada.

item.title: High fossil fuel prices spread inflation ‘like a cancer’, UN climate negotiator tells Cop31
item.description: Simon Stiell makes opening address at summit in Turkey, where talks are under way about speeding up shift to electrification A global fossil fuel price crisis is “spreading inflation like a cancer” around the planet, the UN’s chief climate negotiator, Simon Stiell, told the opening plenary of critical UN climate talks in Turkey. Stiell joined Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia, which is leading the negotiations, in promoting renewable energy and a new electrification goal as an optimistic alternative to a planet still tied to oil, coal and gas. Continue reading... Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.description: Mid-power (3-7 kW) Hall effect thruster systems have been identified by government and industry stakeholders as critical capabilities for satellite, defense, and exploration missions. Given the need for this capability, NASA is launching the Advanced Mid-Power Electric Rocket (AMPERE) Challenge. The NASA AMPERE Challenge invites U.S. commercial companies to develop and demonstrate mid-power Hall effect […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Two nearby rocky worlds could offer alien astronomers views of planets appearing to reverse course
item.description: Aliens have long been a staple of science fiction. Yet the possibility of intelligent life beyond Earth is more than a matter of imagination—it is also a subject of serious scientific inquiry. Professor Woong-bae Zee of Sejong University's School of Liberal Studies has recently published an astronomy paper that places the word "alien" front and center. Fuente: Phys.org.

En el marco de una edad de oro de […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: The fastest levitated spinning magnet ever made might help physicists search for dark matter
item.description: Tiny levitated magnets are able to avoid contact friction, making them useful for detecting extremely weak forces and magnetic fields and acting as ultralow-noise quantum sensors and precision measurement tools. Combining levitation with extreme cold further reduces unwanted motion that can make faint signals hard to detect. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Satellite monitoring of the world's oceans is being restricted by legal barriers, study suggests
item.description: Satellite technology can increasingly track vessels across the world's oceans and has the ability to detect industrial fishing inside marine protected areas (MPAs). But new research has suggested that regulations governing these often vulnerable parts of our planet could be preventing global authorities from turning satellite detection into effective enforcement. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Repeated racism linked to depression and suicidal thoughts in Colorado teens
item.description: Knowing that multiple studies provide strong evidence that links racism to poor mental health, researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz wanted to know what types of racist incidents young people are experiencing in schools and if repeated events were more harmful to their mental health. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The art of good conversation may involve a little pink noise
item.description: Most of us like a good old chat with friends, colleagues, neighbors or acquaintances. But what can turn a really good chat into a great one? Sure, conversation topics matter, but scientists have found underlying patterns that may explain our best interactions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Prehistoric whale reveals extreme skull asymmetry
item.description: Sperm whales and pygmy sperm whales are known among mammals for their unusually shaped heads. Unlike most vertebrates, which are bilaterally symmetrical, toothed whales have asymmetrical skulls that accommodate highly specialized organs used for echolocation and sound production. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Astronauts Across Generations Share the Stage
item.description: On Nov. 6, 2026, Purpose Entertainment hosted the Artemis Celebration Gala at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Merritt Island, Florida. Held on the eve of NASA’s MAX POWER event, the gala celebrated the explorers, innovators, and visionaries advancing the next era of human spaceflight. The event honored the successful completion of the agency’s […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Gary Daines

item.title: 'Nice' by any other name means essentially the same thing
item.description: Is any good deed truly selfless—and does it matter? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cells 'sense' physical forces to seal tissues and protect organs
item.description: Northwestern Medicine scientists have uncovered a molecular mechanism that enables cells to protect organs from leaks, infection and inflammation, according to a study published in the Journal of Cell Biology. The findings of the study add to scientific understanding of how epithelial cells maintain protective barriers, said senior author Cara J. Gottardi, professor of medicine in the Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care and of cell and developmental biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why demand persists for the horn of a once near-extinct antelope
item.description: Family traditions, misconceptions about where it comes from, and a belief that remedies sold in shops are government-approved help explain continued demand for saiga antelope horn in Singapore, according to a University of Oxford–led study published in People and Nature. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Seismic imaging reveals double slab tearing at a subduction–collision transition
item.description: An international research team has used seismic imaging to identify two slab tears beneath the Zagros–Makran transition zone located in southeastern Iran near the Strait of Hormuz. The findings suggest that the tears formed through distinct geodynamic mechanisms and may have influenced regional tectonic deformation and magmatic activity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: MAX POWER: NASA’s Inaugural Aerospace Expo Ignites America’s Future
item.description: Thousands gathered over several days in early November to experience MAX POWER – NASA’s first exhibition of America’s superiority in space, aeronautics, and technology on and around the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The multi-day, family-friendly event honored the nation’s 250th anniversary and served as a culmination of the agency’s Inspiration Tour. Among the […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau

item.title: NASA’s ESCAPADE Completes Powered Earth Flybys, Now En Route to Mars
item.description: NASA’s two ESCAPADE (Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers) spacecraft have each successfully completed a powered Earth flyby, using Earth’s gravity in combination with a sustained engine burn to slingshot themselves toward Mars. With these successful maneuvers complete, the twin spacecraft are on target to reach the Red Planet in September 2027. “This is […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: La Tierra tiene una invitada por Navidad: una miniluna de dos metros que vino en abril y se irá después de las fiestas
item.description: Estas Navidades, la Tierra tendrá una invitada muy especial. Una miniluna que vino a visitarnos el pasado mes de abril y que ha decidido quedarse hasta que pasen las fiestas. Obviamente, las rocas espaciales no deciden nada, permíteme la licencia literaria. Este objeto fue detectado orbitando a nuestro planeta en agosto de este año, aunque los cálculos de su trayectoria han demostrado que llevaba junto a nosotros cuatro meses. Estos mismos cálculos señalan que seguirá dando vueltas a nuestro alrededor más o menos hasta después de Navidad. Para principios de 2027 ya se habría marchado, aunque… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Watching others pays off: Attentive macaques benefit from observing their group mates interacting
item.description: Monkeys constantly observe and evaluate their social environment. It stands to reason that the social and mental abilities required to do so were favored by evolution. After all, these abilities should influence how an animal interacts with its conspecifics and, as a result, what social position it can attain within the group's hierarchy. Researchers from the DPZ and the University of Göttingen have now investigated whether this widely held assumption is correct by studying 46 wild male Assamese macaques in Thailand. The paper is published in the journal Current Biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Promising new biomarkers to diagnose feline chronic kidney disease
item.description: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is common in cats but often goes undiagnosed until it's at a late stage. Thanks to a recent study published in the Journal of Proteome Research, researchers have new leads to determine how feline CKD develops. The paper reports collections of potential protein biomarkers in urine that could help veterinarians detect different stages of the disease and develop more targeted and effective treatments for this irreversible ailment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: French police officers on trial over beating of black man they accused of not wearing Covid mask
item.description: Assault on Michel Zecler in 2020 is rare case of police brutality reaching court, at time of heightened tensions Three French police officers have gone on trial over the beating of a black music producer who they say was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic, in a rare case of police brutality reaching court. The assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, triggered outrage in France over police violence, which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions claim is limited to isolated cases. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Agence France-Presse

item.title: Interdisciplinarity on the curriculum—teachers hold different views on what students should learn
item.description: The climate transition, energy supply and technological development are just some examples of areas where knowledge from several disciplines needs to come together to find relevant solutions. Engineering students are therefore often given the opportunity to work on interdisciplinary projects. But the term "interdisciplinary" encompasses widely differing ideas about what the teaching should involve and what students are actually expected to learn. This is shown by a study in which researchers interviewed 18 teachers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, Aalto University in Finland… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chirality of 'trions' illuminates new paths for quantum optics
item.description: Scientists from Tokyo Metropolitan University have discovered that charged states made of two electrons and a positively charged hole (or vice versa) on atomically thin rolls of carbon atoms have a structure-derived "handedness" in how they interact with light. While electron-hole pairs, or "excitons," were known to keep the chirality of the underlying nanotube, the team showed that adding a charge to create "trions" does not change this property. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How bacteria build the molecular bushing of the flagellar motor
item.description: The bacterial flagellum is a motility organelle that enables bacteria to swim and is composed of more than 30 different proteins. Researchers have long sought to understand how this complex nanomachine self-assembles from many parts in the correct order and at the correct positions. In a study published in Communications Biology, a research team at the University of Osaka revealed the mechanism by which the flagellar motor assembles its bushing around the drive shaft. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Protecting the vulnerable Y chromosome at the beginning of development
item.description: It's known that the Y chromosome, which confers male sex, plays a big role in development and health, despite its small size. As cells age they frequently lose their Y chromosomes, which is associated with conditions like cancer, Alzheimer's disease and heart disease. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: COP31 summit targets major electrification push as 1.5C goal slips away
item.description: The climate summit will push for nations around the world to electrify their energy faster and move away from fossil fuels, as Chris Bowen predicts global temperatures will rise to 2.6 degrees above pre-industrial levels. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Laura Tingle

item.title: Investigadores de Paraguay intentan abrir la bóveda oculta en la mansión de Santiago Peña
item.description: El fiscal señaló que analizan llevar a la ex primera dama para acceder a la caja fuerte de alta seguridad o incluso una detonación controlada Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: Ancient underwater canyons reveal clues to the world's oldest animal life
item.description: Geologists have uncovered new evidence that dramatic sea-level changes carved giant underwater canyons in South Australia's Flinders Ranges hundreds of millions of years ago, helping to create conditions that preserved some of the earliest complex life on Earth. The findings, led by Adelaide University, shed new light on the environmental changes that accompanied the rise of the mysterious Ediacaran biota. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Removing too much crop waste for bioenergy could come at a cost to biodiversity, study finds
item.description: Crop residues—the stems, leaves and husks left behind after harvesting cereals—could provide an important source of renewable energy for Europe, but research led by the University of Surrey suggests that removing too much from fields could come at a cost to biodiversity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Lentejas de Canadá y alubias argentinas: la realidad detrás de platos tradicionales como las fabes asturianas
item.description: Un buen cocido madrileño , un potaje de vigilia , una fabada asturiana o un plato de judiones de La Granja . Todo suena tradicional y muy típico de la gastronomía patria, pero la realidad es que gran parte de las legumbres que usamos en algunos de nuestros potajes más emblemáticos tienen poco que ver con el campo español: llegan de cientos (o incluso miles) de kilómetros de distancia, de plantaciones de Norteamérica u otras zonas de Europa. De hecho, cuando hablamos de ciertas legumbres lo más fácil es encontrarse con género extranjero, no autóctono. La razón es muy sencilla: costes. ¿Te… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Inicia COP31 Turquía- Australia con los combustibles fósiles y la energía en el centro del debate
item.description: La transición energética, los combustibles fósiles y la electrificación vuelven a ser temas centrales de la agenda de la COP31 en Turquía y copresidida por Australia. Entre otros temas que juegan un papel importante de los debates también se encuentra la guerra en Irán, que aumentó los precios globales del petróleo. Nuestro enviado especial, Adrià Rocha, se encuentra en la ciudad de Antalya, que ejerce como anfitrión oficial, mientras las negociaciones oficiales se realizarán en territorio australiano. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: Two genes, two harvests: Adapting barley for double cropping
item.description: Growing two crops in succession on the same land requires a tight schedule. In parts of central and eastern China, farmers sow barley in autumn and harvest it in late spring. It is then followed by a summer crop, such as rice. For this cropping sequence to succeed, the barley must mature in time. An early harvest also helps the crop avoid heat and rain toward the end of the growing season. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: COP31: Betting on electricity to break the climate deadlock
item.description: From November 9 to 20, the international community is gathering in Antalya, Turkey, for the UN COP31 conference. At a time when the energy crisis linked to the war in the Middle East has forced countries to confront their dependence on fossil fuels, this new round of climate negotiations is starting off with a new goal: to push for a massive shift toward electricity. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: Cyrielle CABOT

item.title: The migration that remade Africa
item.description: It's not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between A.D. 1000 and 1700—were masters. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: COP31 opens with leaders under pressure to tackle climate crisis
item.description: The COP31 climate talks kicked off Monday with an early fight over money as the U.N.'s chief urged world leaders to "get serious" about tackling the crisis after a year of devastating weather extremes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A hummingbird's brilliant magenta feathers depend on a hidden middle layer
item.description: The brilliant magenta feathers on the head and throat of a male Anna's hummingbird present an optical puzzle. Magenta cannot be produced by a single wavelength of light. Instead, the feathers reflect a mixture of red and blue. Scientists understood the strong red reflection, but the weaker blue component was harder to explain. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover
item.description: Scientists have discovered that pantethine, a readily available vitamin B5 derivative, can calm overactive immune cells and may help fight psoriasis. The supplement prevented psoriasis in mice and showed promising results in a small human trial, revealing an unexpected connection between cholesterol and autoimmune inflammation. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: When your gut bacteria run out of fiber, they may start eating your gut lining
item.description: Scientists have discovered that gut bacteria can feed on the protective mucus lining your intestines, producing potentially harmful compounds, but fiber helps keep this activity in check. Overlooked proteins in plant foods also help shift gut bacteria toward producing beneficial substances, revealing a surprising new reason plant-based diets may be good for you. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A quantum breakthrough makes light behave like both a solid and a liquid
item.description: Scientists have observed a bizarre quantum state of matter that combines the structure of a crystal with the frictionless flow of a liquid, all at room temperature. The breakthrough overturns a major practical limitation of exotic quantum experiments and could help bring powerful new light-based computing and sensing technologies closer to reality. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: CHAPEA Mission 2 Crew Reflects After 378 Days on Simulated Mars
item.description: After 378 days without windows, the sounds of the outside world, or real-time calls with family and friends, four research volunteers stepped out of NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat on Oct. 31, completing the agency’s second yearlong Mars surface simulation. Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, James Spicer, and Matthew Montgomery entered the roughly 1,700-square-foot, 3D-printed habitat at […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Sumer Loggins

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease
item.description: After more than 35 years of research, scientists have uncovered surprising clues about what really drives Lyme disease risk. Contrary to longstanding assumptions, deer populations appear less important than mice, which can fuel a 40% increase in tick numbers the following year. Even acorn production can predict tick population surges two years in advance, while extreme temperatures may be far less deadly to ticks than scientists once believed. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer
item.description: A surprising new study from UCLA suggests that a naturally occurring molecule could help breast cancer survivors overcome the frustrating brain fog and exhaustion that can linger long after treatment ends. Researchers found that women taking an oxaloacetate supplement for eight weeks experienced substantial improvements in memory, concentration, mental clarity, and fatigue. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Caltech robot makes history by building a structure in space
item.description: For the first time, a robot has autonomously built part of a structure in space, demonstrating a breakthrough that could fundamentally change space exploration. The technology could one day allow scientists to construct enormous telescopes, communications antennas, and solar power stations in orbit, far beyond the size limits of today's rockets. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: NASA reveals bold new plan to return astronauts to the Moon in 2028
item.description: NASA has revealed an accelerated plan to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing competing lunar landers and a crucial orbital test scheduled for 2027. Faster rocket preparations, new lightweight spacesuits, and redesigned missions could help pave the way for a permanent lunar presence and future human exploration of Mars. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study
item.description: A massive study of more than 120,000 older adults suggests that common osteoporosis drugs may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias by up to 24%. The surprising findings raise the possibility that medications already used to strengthen bones could also help protect the aging brain. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Doctors are using bacteria-killing viruses against superbugs that drugs cannot beat
item.description: Amidst the rising concern over antibiotic resistance, doctors are turning to phage therapy, a novel approach that employs viruses to target and eliminate dangerous bacteria. A recent Belgian study found that over 77% of patients showed significant clinical improvement. To enhance the application of personalized bacteriophage treatments, new international guidelines have been introduced, though researchers underline the importance of further studies to comprehend the therapy's potential fully. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
item.description: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate. Fuente: ScienceDaily.
